section.heading: 8.3 Convex Combinations
section.paragraph: Section 8.1 considered special linear combinations of the form
$$c_{1} \mathbf{v}_{1} + c_{2} \mathbf{v}_{2} + \hdots + c_{k} \mathbf{v}_{k} , & \text{where} & c_{1} + c_{2} + \hdots + c_{k} = 1$$
This section further restricts the weights to be nonnegative.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: A convex combination of points $$\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{k}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is a linear combination of the form

such that $$c_{1} + c_{2} + \cdots + c_{k} = 1$$ and $$c_{i} \geq 0$$ for all $$i$$ . The set of all convex combinations of points in a set $$S$$ is called the convex hull of $$S$$ , denoted by $$\text{conv} S$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: The convex hull of a single point $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ is just the set $$\left\{ \textbf{v}_{1} \right\}$$ , the same as the affine hull. In other cases, the convex hull is properly contained in the affine hull. Recall that the affine hull of distinct points $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ is the line
$$\mathbf{y} = \left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right) \mathbf{v}_{1} + t \mathbf{v}_{2} , & \text{with} t \text{in} \mathbb{R}$$
Because the weights in a convex combination are nonnegative, the points in $$\text{conv\{} \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2} \text{\}}$$ may be written as
$$\mathbf{y} = \left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right) \mathbf{v}_{1} + t \mathbf{v}_{2} , & \text{with} \text{0} \leq t \leq 1$$
which is the line segment between $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , hereafter denoted by $$\overset{‾}{\textbf{v}_{1}\textbf{v}_{2}}$$ .﻿

If a set $$S$$ is affinely independent and if $$\textbf{p} \in \text{aff} S$$ , then $$\mathbf{p} \in \text{conv} S$$ if and only if the barycentric coordinates of $$\textbf{p}$$ are nonnegative. Example 1 shows a special situation in which $$S$$ is much more than just affinely independent.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Let

$$v_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}3 \\ 0 \\ 6 \\ - 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & v_{2} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 6 \\ 3 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & v_{3} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}3 \\ 6 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & p_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & p_{2} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 10 \\ 5 \\ 11 \\ - 4\end{matrix} \left]\right. ,$$

and $$S = \left\{ \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\textbf{v}_{3} \right\}$$ . Note that $$S$$ is an orthogonal set. Determine whether $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ is in $$\text{Span} S$$ , $$\text{aff} S$$ , and $$\text{conv} S$$ . Then do the same for $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ .﻿
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: If $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ is at least a linear combination of the points in $$S$$ , then the weights are easily found, because $$S$$ is an orthogonal set. Let $$W$$ be the subspace spanned by $$S$$ . A calculation as in Section 6.3 shows that the orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ onto $$W$$ is $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ itself:

$$\text{proj} _{W } \mathbf{p}_{1} & = & \frac{\mathbf{p}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{1}}{\mathbf{v}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{1}} \mathbf{v}_{1} + \frac{\mathbf{p}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{2}}{\mathbf{v}_{2} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{2}} \mathbf{v}_{2} + \frac{\mathbf{p}_{1} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{3}}{\mathbf{v}_{3} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{3}} \mathbf{v}_{3} & = & \frac{18}{54} \mathbf{v}_{1} + \frac{18}{54} \mathbf{v}_{2} + \frac{18}{54} \mathbf{v}_{3} & = & \frac{1}{3} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}3 \\ 0 \\ 6 \\ - 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. + \frac{1}{3} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 6 \\ 3 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. + \frac{1}{3} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}3 \\ 6 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \mathbf{p}_{1}$$

This shows that $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ is in $$\text{Span} S$$ . Also, since the coefficients sum to $$1$$ , $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ is in $$\text{aff} S$$ . In fact, $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ is in $$\text{conv} S,$$ because the coefficients are also nonnegative.

For $$\mathbf{p}_{2}$$ , a similar calculation shows that $$\text{proj} _{W}\mathbf{p}_{2} \neq \mathbf{p}_{2}$$ . Since $$\text{proj} _{W}\mathbf{p}_{2}$$ is the closest point in $$\text{Span} S$$ to $$\mathbf{p}_{2}$$ , the point $$\mathbf{p}_{2}$$ is not in $$\text{Span} S$$ . In particular, $$\mathbf{p}_{2}$$ cannot be in $$\text{aff} S$$ or $$\text{conv} S$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: Recall that a set $$S$$ is affine if it contains all lines determined by pairs of points in $$S$$ . When attention is restricted to convex combinations, the appropriate condition involves line segments rather than lines.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: A set $$S$$ is convex if for each $$\textbf{p}$$ , $$\textbf{q} \in S$$ , the line segment $$\overline{\mathbf{pq}}$$ is contained in $$S$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: Intuitively, a set $$S$$ is convex if every two points in the set can “see” each other without the line of sight leaving the set. Figure 1 illustrates this idea.

image.alt: Three solids with a line segment inside each of them.

section.paragraph: The next result is analogous to Theorem 2 for affine sets.

note.title: ﻿﻿Theorem ﻿7﻿
note.heading: ﻿﻿Theorem ﻿7﻿
note.paragraph: A set $$S$$ is convex if and only if every convex combination of points of $$S$$ lies in $$S$$ . That is, $$S$$ is convex if and only if $$S = \text{conv} S$$ .﻿

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: The argument is similar to the proof of Theorem 2. The only difference is in the induction step. When taking a convex combination of $$k + 1$$ points, consider $$\textbf{y} = c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1} + \cdots + c_{k}\textbf{v}_{k} + c_{k + 1}\textbf{v}_{k + 1}$$ , where $$c_{1} + \cdots + c_{k + 1} = 1$$ and $$0 \leq c_{i} \leq 1$$ for all $$i$$ . If $$c_{k + 1} = 1$$ , then $$\textbf{y} = \textbf{v}_{k + 1}$$ , which belongs to $$S$$ , and there is nothing further to prove. If $$c_{k + 1} < 1$$ , let $$t = c_{1} + \cdots + c_{k}$$ . Then $$t = 1 - c_{k + 1} > 0$$ and
$$\textbf{y} = ( 1 - c_{k + 1} ) \left(\frac{c_{1}}{t} \textbf{v}_{1} + \hdots + \frac{c_{k}}{t} \textbf{v}_{k}\right) + c_{k + 1} \textbf{v}_{k + 1}$$

By the induction hypothesis, the point $$\textbf{z} = (c_{1}/t)\textbf{v}_{1} + \cdots + (c_{k}/t)\textbf{v}_{k}$$ is in $$S$$ , since the nonnegative coefficients sum to $$1$$ . Thus equation (1) displays $$\textbf{y}$$ as a convex combination of two points in $$S$$ . By the principle of induction, every convex combination of such points lies in $$S$$ .﻿

Theorem 9 below provides a more geometric characterization of the convex hull of a set. It requires a preliminary result on intersections of sets. Recall from Section 4.1 (Exercise 40) that the intersection of two subspaces is itself a subspace. In fact, the intersection of any collection of subspaces is itself a subspace. A similar result holds for affine sets and convex sets.

note.title: ﻿﻿Theorem ﻿8﻿
note.heading: ﻿﻿Theorem ﻿8﻿
note.paragraph: Let $$\{ S_{\alpha}:\alpha \in A\}$$ be any collection of convex sets. Then $$\cap_{\alpha \in A}S_{\alpha}$$ is convex. If $$\{ T_{\beta}:\beta \in B\}$$ is any collection of affine sets, then $$\cap_{\beta \in B}T_{\beta}$$ is affine.

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: If $$\textbf{p}$$ and $$\textbf{q}$$ are in $$\cap S_{\alpha}$$ , then $$\textbf{p}$$ and $$\textbf{q}$$ are in each $$S_{\alpha}$$ . Since each $$S_{\alpha}$$ is convex, the line segment between $$\textbf{p}$$ and $$\textbf{q}$$ is in $$S_{\alpha}$$ for all $$\alpha$$ and hence that segment is contained in $$\cap S_{\alpha}$$ . The proof of the affine case is similar.

note.title: Theorem ﻿9﻿
note.heading: Theorem ﻿9﻿
note.paragraph: For any set $$S$$ , the convex hull of $$S$$ is the intersection of all the convex sets that contain $$S$$ .﻿

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: Let $$T$$ denote the intersection of all the convex sets containing $$S$$ . Since $$\text{conv} S$$ is a convex set containing $$S$$ , it follows that $$T \subseteq \text{conv} S$$ . On the other hand, let $$C$$ be any convex set containing $$S$$ . Then $$C$$ contains every convex combination of points of $$C$$ (Theorem 7), and hence also contains every convex combination of points of the subset $$S$$ . That is, $$\text{conv} S \subseteq C$$ . Since this is true for every convex set $$C$$ containing $$S$$ , it is also true for the intersection of them all. That is, $$\text{conv} S \subseteq T .$$

Theorem 9 shows that $$\text{conv} S$$ is in a natural sense the “smallest” convex set containing $$S$$ . For example, consider a set $$S$$ that lies inside some large rectangle in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ , and imagine stretching a rubber band around the outside of $$S$$ . As the rubber band contracts around $$S$$ , it outlines the boundary of the convex hull of $$S$$ . Or to use another analogy, the convex hull of $$S$$ fills in all the holes in the inside of $$S$$ and fills out all the dents in the boundary of $$S$$ .﻿

Then $$\text{conv} S$$ is a triangular surface in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ , with vertices $$\textbf{e}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{e}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{e}_{3}$$ . See Figure 2.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Let $$S = \left\{ {\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}:x \geq 0{and}y = x^{2}} \right\}$$ . Show that the convex hull of $$S$$ is the union of the origin and $$\left\{ {\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}:x > 0{and}y \geq x^{2}} \right\}$$ . See Figure 3.

image.alt: A graph shows a half parabola in the first quadrant given by the equation y equals x squared.

example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Every point in $$\text{conv} S$$ must lie on a line segment that connects two points of $$S$$ . The dashed line in Figure 3 indicates that, except for the origin, the positive $$y \text{-axis}$$ is not in $$\text{conv} S$$ , because the origin is the only point of $$S$$ on the $$y \text{-axis}$$ . It may seem reasonable that Figure 3 does show $$\text{conv} S,$$ but how can you be sure that the point $$(10^{- 2},10^{4})$$ , for example, is on a line segment from the origin to a point on the curve in $$S$$ ?
Consider any point $$\textbf{p}$$ in the shaded region of Figure 3, say
$$\mathbf{p} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}a \\ b\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & \text{with} a > 0 \text{and} b \geq a^{2}$$

The line through $$\textbf{0}$$ and $$\textbf{p}$$ has the equation $$y = (b/a)t$$ for $$t$$ real. That line intersects $$S$$ where $$t$$ satisfies $$(b/a)t = t^{2},$$ that is, when $$t = b/a.$$ Thus, $$\textbf{p}$$ is on the line segment from $$0$$ to $$\begin{bmatrix} {b/a} \\ {b^{2}/a^{2}} \end{bmatrix}$$ , which shows that Figure 3 is correct.

section.paragraph: The following theorem is basic in the study of convex sets. It was first proved by Constantin Caratheodory in 1907. If $$\textbf{p}$$ is in the convex hull of $$S$$ , then, by definition, $$\textbf{p}$$ must be a convex combination of points of $$S$$ . But the definition makes no stipulation as to how many points of $$S$$ are required to make the combination. Caratheodory’s remarkable theorem says that in an $$n \text{-dimensional}$$ space, the number of points of $$S$$ in the convex combination never has to be more than $$n + 1$$ .﻿

note.title: Theorem 10
note.heading: Theorem 10
note.paragraph: (Caratheodory) If $$S$$ is a nonempty subset of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , then every point in $$\text{conv} S$$ can be expressed as a convex combination of $$n + 1$$ or fewer points of $$S$$ .﻿

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: Given $$\textbf{p}$$ in $$\text{conv} S$$ , one may write $$\textbf{p} = c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1} + \cdots + c_{k}\textbf{v}_{k}$$ , where $$\textbf{v}_{i} \in S$$ , $$c_{1} + \cdots + c_{k} = 1$$ , and $$c_{i} \geq 0$$ , for some $$k$$ and $$i = 1,\ldots,k$$ . The goal is to show that such an expression exists for $$\textbf{p}$$ with $$k \leq n + 1$$ .﻿
If $$k > n + 1$$ , then $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{k}\}$$ is affinely dependent, by Exercise 20 in Section 8.2. Thus there exist scalars $$d_{1},\ldots,d_{k}$$ , not all zero, such that
Consider the two equations
$$c_{1} \textbf{v}_{1} + c_{2} \textbf{v}_{2} + \hdots + c_{k} \textbf{v}_{k} = \textbf{p}$$
and
$$d_{1} \textbf{v}_{1} + d_{2} \textbf{v}_{2} + \hdots + d_{k} \textbf{v}_{k} = \textbf{0}$$

By subtracting an appropriate multiple of the second equation from the first, we now eliminate one of the $$\textbf{v}_{i}$$ terms and obtain a convex combination of fewer than $$k$$ elements of $$S$$ that is equal to $$\textbf{p}$$ .﻿

Since not all of the $$d_{i}$$ coefficients are zero, we may assume (by reordering subscripts if necessary) that $$d_{k} > 0$$ and that $$c_{k}/d_{k} \leq c_{i}/d_{i}$$ for all those $$i$$ for which $$d_{i} > 0$$ . For $$i = 1,\ldots,k$$ , let $$b_{i} = c_{i} - \left( c_{k}/d_{k} \right)d_{i}$$ . Then $$b_{k} = 0$$ and

Furthermore, each $$b_{i} \geq 0$$ . Indeed, if $$d_{i} \leq 0$$ , then $$b_{i} \geq c_{i} \geq 0$$ . If $$d_{i} > 0$$ , then $$b_{i} =$$ $$d_{i}\left( c_{i}/d_{i} - c_{k}/d_{k} \right) \geq 0$$ . By construction,

$$\sum_{i = 1}^{k - 1} b_{i} \mathbf{v}_{i} & = & \sum_{i = 1}^{k} b_{i} \mathbf{v}_{i} = \sum_{i = 1}^{k} \left(\right. c_{i} - \frac{c_{k}}{d_{k}} d_{i} \left.\right) \mathbf{v}_{i} & = & \sum_{i = 1}^{k} c_{i} \mathbf{v}_{i} - \frac{c_{k}}{d_{k}} \sum_{i = 1}^{k} d_{i} \mathbf{v}_{i} = \sum_{i = 1}^{k} c_{i} \mathbf{v}_{i} = \mathbf{p}$$

Thus $$\textbf{p}$$ is now a convex combination of $$k - 1$$ of the points $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{k}$$ . This process may be repeated until $$\textbf{p}$$ is expressed as a convex combination of at most $$n + 1$$ of the points of $$S$$ .﻿
The following example illustrates the calculations in the proof above.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Let

$$\mathbf{v}_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & \mathbf{v}_{2} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 \\ 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & \mathbf{v}_{3} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}5 \\ 4\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & \mathbf{v}_{4} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}3 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. , & & \mathbf{p} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\frac{10}{3} \\ \frac{5}{2}\end{matrix} \left]\right. ,$$
and $$S = \left\{ \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\textbf{v}_{3},\textbf{v}_{4} \right\}$$ . Then
$$\frac{1}{4} \textbf{v}_{1} + \frac{1}{6} \textbf{v}_{2} + \frac{1}{2} \textbf{v}_{3} + \frac{1}{12} \textbf{v}_{4} = \textbf{p}$$
Use the procedure in the proof of Caratheodory’s Theorem to express $$\textbf{p}$$ as a convex combination of three points of $$S$$ .﻿
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The set $$S$$ is affinely dependent. Use the technique of Section 8.2 to obtain an affine dependence relation
$$- 5 \textbf{v}_{1} + 4 \textbf{v}_{2} - 3 \textbf{v}_{3} + 4 \textbf{v}_{4} = \textbf{0}$$

Next, choose the points $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{4}$$ in (3), whose coefficients are positive. For each point, compute the ratio of the coefficients in equations (2) and (3). The ratio for $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ is $$\frac{1}{6} \div 4 = \frac{1}{24}$$ , and that for $$\textbf{v}_{4}$$ is $$\frac{1}{12} \div 4 = \frac{1}{48}$$ . The ratio for $$\textbf{v}_{4}$$ is smaller, so subtract $$\frac{1}{48}$$ times equation (3) from equation (2) to eliminate $$\textbf{v}_{4}$$ :

$$\left(\frac{1}{4} + \frac{5}{48}\right) \textbf{v}_{1} + \left(\frac{1}{6} - \frac{4}{48}\right) \textbf{v}_{2} + \left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{3}{48}\right) \textbf{v}_{3} + \left(\frac{1}{12} - \frac{4}{48}\right) \textbf{v}_{4} = \textbf{p} \frac{17}{48} \textbf{v}_{1} + \frac{4}{48} \textbf{v}_{2} + \frac{27}{48} \textbf{v}_{3} = \textbf{p}$$

section.paragraph: This result cannot, in general, be improved by decreasing the required number of points. Indeed, given any three non-collinear points in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ , the centroid of the triangle formed by them is in the convex hull of all three, but is not in the convex hull of any two.

list.item: Let $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ 1 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{3} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 2} \\ 4 \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\textbf{p}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ , and $$\textbf{p}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ , and let $$S = \left{\right. \textbf{v}_{1} , \textbf{v}_{2} ,$$ $$\left. \textbf{v}_{3} \right\}$$ . Determine whether $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ are in $$\text{conv} S$$ .﻿
Let $$S$$ be the set of points on the curve $$y = 1/x$$ for $$x > 0$$ . Explain geometrically why $$\text{conv} S$$ consists of all points on and above the curve $$S$$ .﻿
